#5027. Why the Path to Quantum Resistance Runs Uphill for Bitcoin Wallet Makers

Why the Path to Quantum Resistance Runs Uphill for Bitcoin Wallet Makers

Bitcoin custody has always involved some degree of risk, but wallet manufacturers like Trezor—which build physical devices designed to keep a user’s private keys secure offline—are preparing for a post-quantum world where new challenges arise.

That’s because SHRINCS, the community’s leading candidate for a post-quantum signature scheme, allows users to make transactions using stateful signatures that require rigid state tracking to prevent funds from being stolen, according to Trezor CTO Tomáš Sušánka.

Proposed late last year by Blockstream Research Director Jonas Nick and cryptographer Mikhail Kudinov, SHRINCS centers on a composite hash-based approach: users can make transactions using either stateful signatures or stateless signatures.

Stateless signatures are quite large—potentially affecting fees, signature speed, and other efficiency metrics—but are safe to reuse, while smaller, more efficient stateful signatures come with serious security risks when reused beyond a particular signing budget.

The stateful component of SHRINCS is made up of a tree of one-time signatures, and if these keys are accidentally used more than once, enough cryptographic information is revealed for someone else to forge that user’s signature and effectively steal funds.

If Bitcoin successfully adopts SHRINCS, maintaining a meticulous count of the wallet’s state will become a critical responsibility for wallet developers—with lots of potential edge-case security risks.

“You’re giving them an option to mess up,” Sušánka said during a recent episode of MARA Foundation TV, in reference to state tracking. “It’s our job to make it in a secure way, right? It shouldn't be the user’s job.”

To mitigate this risk, Trezor is weighing options for how to support secure UX in a post-quantum world. For instance, Sušánka said the company is considering making the heavier, slower stateless signatures the default setting for all users, tucking the riskier stateful option behind an advanced settings wall.

While Sušánka recognizes that SHRINCS may be the conservative cryptographic choice because it relies on the same cryptographic assumptions as SHA-256, he is “kind of torn on the topic because maintaining the state is a burden.”

“For example, you can have two Trezors with the same recovery seed. How do you share the state between those two? You really don’t,” he added.

“That being said, as it is with everything, this is about trade-offs,” Sušánka continued. “The [stateful] signatures are 10 times smaller ... That makes a big difference. So, I just don't want to throw it off the table completely.”

Sušánka went on to share that while many are focused on Bitcoin’s migration path to post-quantum addresses and signatures, hardware wallet devices will also need to be physically updated for full quantum protection. Most signing devices use quantum-vulnerable cryptography for hardware-specific security functions, like firmware and device authentication.

If users want to ensure their devices are secure in a post-quantum world, they will need to use “quantum-ready” devices—that is, devices that use post-quantum cryptography for device and firmware authentication as well.

In anticipation of these needs, the company is already shipping products like Trezor Safe 7 that support post-quantum cryptography for wallet authentication processes. Of course, transactions made on these devices will only be quantum-secure once Bitcoin itself upgrades to post-quantum security.

That said, Sušánka warned developers not to wait too long to give users migration options, as he believes the migration of potentially millions of users will take time.

“People should be ready to make compromises,” Sušánka said. “If we’re all going to be very strict on what can and cannot be done, we’re not going to get anywhere.”

André Beganski is a Senior Content Manager at MARA Foundation, producing content on topics including the intersection of quantum computing and cryptography. He has previously worked for Decrypt.

#5025. Bitcoin tumbles below $69,000 as Nvidia turmoil adds to Fed-driven market jitters

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

A total of $798 million in crypto positions has been liquidated over the past four hours, including $718.5 million in long positions.

Bitcoin Bitcoin (BTC) and other major cryptocurrencies continued to fall during Asian morning trading as the fallout from Nvidia cofounder Jensen Huang's exit and expectations of a Federal Reserve rate hike weighed on market sentiment.

The world's largest cryptocurrency plunged 7% over the past 24 hours to $68,408 as of 12:10 a.m. ET Friday, its lowest level since Aug. 20, according to The Block's bitcoin price page. Ether Ethereum (ETH) dropped 6% to trade at $1,921. BNB slid 6.3%, while XRP lost 3.5%.

Crypto liquidations totaled $1.47 billion over the past 24 hours, with 175,299 traders liquidated, according to CoinGlass data. Long positions accounted for $1.31 billion of the total. Notably, liquidations totaled $798 million over the past four hours, including $718.5 million in long positions.

"The sharp leg lower in crypto looks like a leverage event as BTC broke key levels," said Rick Maeda, head of markets at Laevitas. "BTC had already lost $72,000 in the U.S. session, and once it broke $70,000 late morning in Asia, the long positions clustered below that level were forced out quickly, with more than $600 million in four hours and over $1.3 billion in the past day."

The market downturn came as traders continued to assess the fallout from Nvidia's leadership shake-up amid expectations of another Fed interest rate hike, analysts said.

On Thursday morning, Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO after the company launched an investigation last weekend into his relationship with a suspected Chinese spy. There had been reports that said Huang engaged in extramarital relationships with an Nvidia executive who reports directly to him and a second Nvidia employee.

"Traders trying to catch a reversal from the Nvidia-driven risk-off, combined with thin bids after this week's CPI, have both played a role in the liquidations," said Maeda.

Meanwhile, BTSE COO Jeff Mei told The Block that bitcoin also fell on assumptions that the Fed would raise rates in December to combat inflation. Mei said traders are watching out for signals of a potential 50-basis-point rate hike, which "hinges on how inflation and unemployment data will trend, as well as oil prices and geopolitical developments in the Middle East."

"If the Fed hikes rates by 50 basis points rather than the expected 25 basis points, bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies could have more room to fall," Mei added.

However, Jeff Ko, chief analyst at ViaBTC, said persistent inflation might actually strengthen bitcoin's appeal as an inflation hedge and bolster the currency debasement trade over the longer term.

"Looking ahead, markets will be closely watching the upcoming PCE in late November, and more importantly, the Dec. 9 FOMC dot plot. As for geopolitics, a de-escalation in Iran could offer one of the quickest paths to bringing inflation down," said Ko.

#5024. The 8 Best Slippers for Women for Max Coziness, Tested By a Style Writer

From couch-rotting to errands, these kicks have you covered.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Now that the weather has cooled down and leaves are on the ground, my style writer brain is in peak outfit mode. I’ve already imagined the ways I’ll wear my leather jackets, chunky knits, and bootcut jeans. But before I start styling my way through the fall and winter, there’s one essential I always reach for first: slippers. I test a lot of shoes in the name of journalism, and few spark more joy than a pair of cute slippers that add the perfect cozy feel to any outfit. Whether I’m channeling my inner couch potato on a lazy Sunday or running errands around town, the best slippers in my stash hit the sweet spot of soft, supportive, and actually stylish.

A lot of the same principles that apply to shopping for supportive sneakers also apply to slippers, says Anne Sharkey, DPM, a podiatrist at Solely Podiatry in Austin, TX. After all, a slipper is the ultimate cozy shoe, but it’s also incredibly useful for keeping your arches happy while walking around hardwood floors at home. That’s why Sharkey says cushioning and arch support are key. Your slippers should feel plush underfoot, but not so squishy that you lose stability. Where you plan to wear them also matters: A pair of house slippers needs less traction and durability than a pair for outdoors, which should have a thicker, more grippy bottom.

After over a year of testing, I found slippers that are plush enough to lounge in, supportive enough for a spin around town, and stylish enough that you’ll actually want to wear them.

When it comes to a slipper that checks every box (plush, supportive, and legitimately stylish), the Ugg Cozy Slipper is the one I always come back to. I’ve been wearing this slipper since fall 2024 with everything from jeans and Henleys to matching sweat sets.

The slipper earns its name with extra-cozy materials, from the sheepskin fur lining to the sweater-knit outer and fluffy collar. I love that it keeps my feet warm and toasty, even during cold winter months. Board-certified foot and ankle surgeon Bobby Pourizaee, DPM says this slipper is excellent for comfort and lounging. Podiatrist and board-certified foot and ankle surgeon Bruce Pinker, DPM agrees, adding that the slip-on style makes this slipper easy to wear.

Beneath the fluff, there’s real structure that keeps my feet fatigue-free. The contoured footbed and firm-yet-plush midsole made with 17 mm of sheepskin hug my arches just right. The outsole is sturdy and grippy, made with dense EVA foam and tons of traction. I wear it on long walks with my dog around the Long Island suburbs and never worry about slipping or falling, no matter the weather. However, it’s still lightweight enough to feel like an indoor slipper.

Pinker says that it could be improved if the heel region were closed for more support and stability, but the easy-on, easy-off fit is part of why I love this slipper. If you’re after something warm, cozy, and super stylish for both indoor and outdoor wear, I can’t recommend this slipper enough.

For a cozy, budget-friendly slipper that doesn’t skimp on comfort, the Dearfoams Lacey Memory Foam Slipper is the one I’ve been living in lately. At under $30, this slipper is way more cushy, warm, and supportive than lots of other house slippers I’ve worn.

I padded around my house in this slipper nonstop for about a year, and it held up beautifully through coffee runs to the kitchen, long hours at my desk, and quick trips to grab packages. It’s definitely a house slipper, but in the best way possible—pure comfort, with just enough structure to feel supportive.

The memory foam cushioning is what makes this slipper so comfortable, Sharkey says. Each step in it feels super plush, molding to the shape of my foot for that “walking on pillows” feel. The fleece lining also keeps my feet cozy without overheating, and the soft knit upper gives it a lounge-all-day kind of vibe that pairs perfectly with pajamas and sweatpants. I absolutely love the heel and arch cushioning, especially when my feet ache after a long day commuting to and from Manhattan, but Sharkey says they should only be worn in the house since they lack the structure needed for long periods on your feet.

But for a house slipper, there’s way more support than I expected. The raised heel area keeps the slipper from sliding off my foot, even when I’m walking up or down stairs. It’s a small but thoughtful feature that makes it feel a bit more secure than your average slip-on. And while the outsole isn’t meant for outdoor adventures, it’s durable enough for quick steps onto the porch or grabbing the mail.

I wore this slipper for nearly a year straight while trodding around my house, and absolutely love them. However, I will say that at about the 10-month mark, they needed to be replaced, as they stretched out a bit and lost some of the much-needed cushioning, support, and traction.

Thanks to its incredible level of cushioning, the Vionic Gemma II Mule Slipper keeps my feet pain-free even after walking in it all day. Pourizaee says it's a strong recommendation thanks to the contoured footbed. The midsole is made from a flexible EVA foam that not only feels super plush under my foot but is designed to absorb shock and reduce stress on the joints. I have lingering ankle and foot pain on one side from a previous high ankle sprain, and while some shoes exacerbate those symptoms, this slipper keeps my feet happy. That comes as no surprise, since this slipper earned an APMA Seal of Acceptance.

It also has great support and stability features. Pinker says it would be improved with a closed-heel design, but I find that the deep heel cup helps, and the strap closure keeps my foot firmly planted—even while speed walking on city sidewalks. Pourizaee adds that the contoured footbed helps keep feet aligned and relieves foot strain. While I often wake up with sore feet that hurt as soon as I step out of bed, I find that when I’ve worn this slipper the day before, foot fatigue is next to zero.

If you like a cozy slipper, the Gemma II delivers. I have the cream color, which is made with a wool upper that keeps my feet warm and looks cute with all my cold-weather loungewear. Other styles have a faux-fur or flannel upper, which also looks super warm and cozy. Plus, since the slipper is designed for indoor and outdoor wear, the synthetic outsole is ultra-durable with a patterned tread design. I’ve even gone for post-rain walks with my dog on wet pavement, and never felt like I was going to slip.

Overall, this slipper is warm, cozy, and ultra-cushioned. It keeps my feet happy with the plush feel underfoot, and I love keeping it by the door when I need a cute shoe to slip on fast.

If you need a slipper with serious arch support, the Orthofeet Charlotte Slipper delivers. Plus, it comes with additional insoles and spacers for days when my feet need extra support.

The Ortho-Cushion system (which includes the removable orthotic insole, ergonomic sole, and fitting spacers) helps to customize the fit and level of cushioning and support. I didn’t realize before selecting my normal size that Orthofeet recommends ordering a half-size down for a more snug fit, but placing the smallest blue fitting spacer (1/16 inch) under the insole kept my foot feeling super secure. Even without any customization, I was impressed by the high level of cushioning that hugs my arches and feels really nice under my heels. The ergonomic sole not only has ample cushioning underfoot, but also the subtle “rocker” design, which refers to a little lift under the heel and toe so those two parts of the shoe don’t touch the ground when standing still, similar to a rocking chair. That shape propels you forward with each step and also helps take some pressure off the joints. Plus, the EVA outsole also has lots of traction patterns to keep every step feeling stable and secure.

I also love the faux fur lining and insole that feels super cozy and keeps my feet warm even while walking outdoors on chilly mornings. The suede outer adds to that cozy vibe and looks super cute. I initially wasn’t sure if this slipper would be my style, but I find myself reaching for it all the time when I leave the house for quick errands and coffee dates with friends. I have the taupe color and often pair it with ankle jeans and sweaters for a comfortable fall fit.

While it does run slightly small, the brand offers half sizes, and the slipper comes with customizable features, so I didn’t find it an issue at all. However, if you’re concerned about fit, I recommend ordering a half size down.

The Sunday Mule Slipper from Bombas is perhaps the most stylish casual shoe that I own. The elongated, oval-toe shape looks super chic, and it's wrapped entirely in a fluffy sherpa material for that cozy-yet-put-together feel. Whether I’m couch-rotting on the weekend, grabbing a latte, or taking a casual stroll around town, I can always count on this slipper. It looks great with a wide-leg lounge pant or leggings with slouchy socks, but I’ve also worn it with a cropped pair of jeans.

Sharkey says it's a good cozy and comfortable option, and that Bombas did a great job with the level of cushioning. That’s thanks to the memory foam footbed, which has a nice squishy feel, contours to the shape of the foot, and softens impact with every step. That contouring feature does wonders for making sure the slipper stays on, even while trekking all around town. However, Sharkey says the backless design does tend to slip off the feet if you’re not careful. I haven’t had any issues there, but it’s something to keep in mind if your feet need an ultra-supportive shoe—in which case, the Orthofeet Charlotte Slipper might be a better choice.

The rubber outsole gives this slip-on shoe a major upgrade, since it helps provide traction when I wear it outside. I keep this slipper mainly for wearing around the house or quick errands, but I have worn it during short, casual walks without worry. The fluffy sherpa material, inside and out, makes it a super cozy option for lazy days cuddled up on the couch and keeps my feet warm even when I take it for a spin outdoors.

Plus, there’s plenty of chic color options. I went with the cream, which I find pairs well with almost anything in my closet—but there’s also a black and brown for additional neutrals, and a dusty purple or tomato red option for something more bold. While this slipper from Bombas might not be the most supportive option, I’d recommend it to anyone looking for a plush, super stylish slipper.

Clogs get a bad rap for making your feet sweat, slide around, and (sorry!) being kind of ugly. But this slip-on clog from Rothy’s nails it on the style front, and is also durable, breathable, and super comfortable. The Casual Clog is well-loved by me and executive editor Abigail Cuffey—oh, and Sharkey recommends it, too.

This slipper/clog hybrid is made with the brand’s signature cushioning made from recycled water bottles and arch support that Sharkey says is ultra comfortable. She also says she likes that the heel cup is a bit deeper than your standard slipper, which helps with stability. I find that the deep heel cup helps cover the back of my foot, so it doesn’t slip off when I’m running around the house doing laundry or walking up and down stairs. The outsole is also made from recycled water bottles and has a grooved design that makes it super durable with tons of traction. I usually wear it for casual outings and meeting up with friends, and find it looks great with baggy jeans and sweaters for a casual-yet-put-together look.

While I own the merino wool version, Cuffey owns both the merino wool and hemp styles. She’s been wearing the hemp clog since fall 2024, and loves that the ultra-cushioned footbed molds to her feet. “It feels like a hug for your heels and toes,” she says. She wears it as a lounge shoe and an outdoor shoe, because of the grippy outsole and substantial feel. Cuffey’s thoughts on the merino wool clog are generally the same, but she loves that the wool feels a little cozier while still airy and breathable. “I usually go through slippers so fast because they get so gross, but Rothy’s Casual Clogs are the first ones that have staying power in my closet,” she says.

It does run a little wide, but the fabric is stretchy, so I haven’t had any issues with it feeling too loose on my feet. But if you’re in between sizes, Rothy’s recommends sizing down for a better fit.

The L.L. Bean Wicked Good Moccasin has become my favorite ever since I got it in the mail. A moccasin is a slipper made of soft leather that wraps around the foot with a single gathered seam at the front. This style is the cushiest, coziest, most supportive I’ve ever worn, earning a permanent spot in my fall and winter footwear rotation.

Unlike some moccasins, Pinker says this style feels especially stable thanks to the rubber outsole with added grip and traction. Plus, the suede material is more structured than other moccasins I’ve worn, which makes for a snug, secure feel. I’ve worn this moccasin weekly over the past month, and I can tell it’s extremely durable. The suede has a lot of heft, and combined with the hand-stitched construction, this moccasin stands up to wear and tear. The fur lining is also extremely comfortable and warm, and I love wearing this shoe on colder days to keep my feet toasty. The insole is also made from the same fur material, which delivers a super plush, cushioned feel underfoot.

There’s also plenty of fur lining the outside of the slipper, which I find super stylish, along with the rawhide laces and bow. It looks great with both joggers and wide-leg sweatpants, and I even wore it recently with cuffed jeans and a boxy sweater for a casual brunch. I have the brown pair, but with seven shades to choose from (including blue, red, and purple!), there’s no shortage of styling potential.

One note: this slipper is spot-clean only, unlike others that can go in the washing machine. However, I wear it nearly every morning lately to walk my dog when the ground is still dewy, and I haven’t gotten any stains that took more than a quick pass with a dry washcloth to remove.

I desperately needed a new house slipper a few weeks ago, so I decided to snag this pair from Fulton—and I couldn’t be happier with my decision. While you could totally get away with wearing this slipper outside (it’s super cute and definitely sturdy), I love keeping this pair inside and free from outside germs—IYKYK.

At first, I honestly wasn’t sure this pair would be a winner: the footbed was super uncomfortable the first day that I wore them. It felt like all the raised areas were in the wrong places, which made it a little difficult to walk. Had I known then that the Fulton website explains there’s a 10-hour break-in process, I’d have been way less concerned.

Lo and behold, by the following day the slippers felt much better—and only continued to get more comfortable as the cork footbed molded to the exact shape of my foot. I wouldn’t call this slipper plush by any means (though the wool upper is quite cozy), so if that’s what you’re looking for, the Ugg, Dearfoams, Orthofeet, or L.L. Bean styles might be better options. But this shoe makes my feet feel so good.

I’ve been suffering from some pretty gnarly foot pain from recently developed plantar fasciitis, but since I started wearing this slipper around the house every day, my feet feel brand new. My arches and heels feel way less achy throughout the day, and it no longer hurts to plant my feet on the ground first thing in the morning.

If you prefer a slide over a slipper, this pick from Oofos is perfect. I often bring it to the gym to wear in the locker room, sauna, or on the way to my post-workout smoothie spot, and the cushy foam insole feels great on my achy feet. As our WH 2025 Fitness Awards winner for Best Recovery Shoe, I had to test it myself for this guide.

Pourizaee says this slide is ideal for recovery or all-day wear thanks to its excellent shock absorption and built-in arch support. That’s because it’s made from the brand's signature OOfoam technology—a springy EVA foam that has plenty of cushion and feels nice and squishy underfoot. The insole’s contoured shape creates built-in arch support, with a high mound near the center that fits perfectly under the arches. That shape reduces stress on the knees, ankles, and other joints. My ankle pain (from a previous sprain) and mysterious knee pain definitely feel better when I wear this slide regularly around the house. Plus, the deep heel cup keeps my foot anchored in place, even when I’m doing housework at lightning speed.

WH executive health and fitness director, Jacqueline Andriakos, swears by it for managing her foot pain, too. "My podiatrist told me I had to get a pair for work-from-home days and going to and from barefoot workout classes," she says. "I notice my chronic foot pain is light years better when I’ve been wearing it more regularly."

Another perk? The foam is water-repellent, odor-resistant, and machine washable. The only feature that would make this slide better, Pinker says, is an ankle strap for extra stability and support.

The right cushioning absorbs impact from walking on hard surfaces to help prevent foot pain, says Pourziaee. All of our favorite slippers have at least a medium level of cushioning.

#5022. Robinhood’s Crypto Trading Volume Falls 48% in October as Event Contracts More Than Double

Crypto trading on Robinhood fell by almost half from a year ago in October, the company said Thursday, as customers traded $17 billion of digital assets while their bets on event contracts more than doubled.

The $17 billion figure was down 21% from September and 48% from October 2025, when crypto notional volume reached $32.5 billion. It covers both the flagship Robinhood app and Bitstamp, the crypto exchange the company bought in 2025.

Volume in the Robinhood app fell to $6.8 billion, down 24% from September and 51% from a year earlier. Bitstamp handled $10.2 billion, down 18% month over month and 45% year over year.

Average daily crypto volume across both platforms came to $548 million, compared with $713 million in September and about $1.05 billion a year ago. Daily average crypto trades slipped to about 700,000 from 900,000 in September and 1.1 million in October 2025.

The contrast with Robinhood’s prediction markets business is stark. Customers traded 5.9 billion event contracts in October, up 5% from September and 136% from the 2.5 billion traded a year earlier. Average daily volume reached 190 million contracts.

Robinhood counts crypto and prediction markets on the same 31-day calendar, since both trade every day, so the comparison is apples to apples. Event contracts let users bet on outcomes such as elections, sports and economic data, and October’s tally covered the final weeks before the Nov. 3 midterm elections.

That growth has drawn scrutiny in Washington. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, who is set to chair the Senate Banking Committee in January, plans to crack down on prediction markets and election betting platforms.

The rest of Robinhood’s brokerage held up better than crypto. Equity notional volume rose 2% from a year earlier to $325 billion, and options contracts traded climbed 8% to 289 million. Margin balances reached $22.9 billion, up 39% year over year.

Funded customers rose by about 130,000 in the month to 28.9 million, and net deposits came to $15.1 billion. Total platform assets slipped 3% from September to $383 billion but were up 12% from a year earlier.

Robinhood did not say why crypto activity fell. The release, like all of the company’s monthly updates, is unaudited and preliminary.

The slump in Robinhood’s crypto numbers lines up with a broader retreat by retail traders. Bitcoin ended September near $83,500 and has slid since, falling below $70,000 early Friday for the first time since August as a hot inflation report raised bets on a Federal Reserve rate hike in December.

Institutional demand has cooled alongside it. U.S. spot bitcoin exchange-traded funds posted a sixth straight day of net outflows on Thursday, and BlackRock’s IBIT, the largest of them, bled about $2 billion over nine sessions through Wednesday. Spot bitcoin ETFs have now erased their net inflows for 2026.

Crypto trading generates transaction revenue for Robinhood, so lower volume generally means fewer fees, even when assets on the platform keep growing. The company reports full fourth-quarter results early next year, and October’s figures are the first look at how the quarter started.

The company has kept expanding its crypto footprint anyway. In October, Robinhood won a license in Dubai to offer bitcoin and stock trading in the Middle East starting in 2027.

Robinhood also said cash and deposit balances fell 20% in October to $16.4 billion, mostly because customers were net buyers, and that the decline has largely reversed in early November. November’s operating data will show whether this month’s selloff below $70,000 brought crypto traders back or pushed more of them toward event contracts.

Arkansas AG Tim Griffin previously sued Kalshi on Nov. 4, alleging that it operated an illegal gambling platform in the state.

The U.S. Department of Justice and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission have filed a lawsuit against Arkansas Attorney General Tim Griffin seeking to block the state's enforcement action against Kalshi, in an escalating legal fight surrounding the prediction market platform.

The federal agencies said that the event contracts targeted by Arkansas are swaps under the CEA, and that the state's efforts to prevent a CFTC-regulated platform from offering such financial products "intrude on the exclusive federal scheme."

The lawsuit comes after Griffin sued Kalshi on Nov. 4, alleging that Kalshi operated an illegal gambling platform allowing users to wager on the outcome of "just about anything."

The Arkansas AG suggested that such "gambling" on Kalshi is "squarely prohibited by Arkansas law."

The DOJ and CFTC are asking the court to grant preliminary and permanent injunctive relief, arguing that Arkansas law is preempted by federal law and can't be enforced against CFTC-regulated prediction market platforms.

The Block has reached out to Kalshi and Griffin's office for comment.

The Arkansas dispute comes amid a growing wave of legal challenges against prediction market platforms across the U.S.

Also on Thursday, Louisiana became the latest state to take on those platforms, with Attorney General Liz Murrill also filing a lawsuit against companies including Kalshi, Polymarket, Robinhood, and Coinbase.

"For too long, they have violated our laws with impunity. No longer: I am seeking an immediate restraining order and an injunction to restore the rule of law in Louisiana," Murrill said in a post on X.

Last week, a federal judge granted a preliminary injunction barring Kalshi from offering sports-event contracts on the lands of two California tribes — Blue Lake Rancheria and the Chicken Ranch Rancheria of Me-Wuk Indians.

A Kalshi spokesperson said the company had voluntarily withdrawn its services from the tribes' lands in September.

#5019. Strategy Made $19.5 Billion in Profit. So Why Is MSCI Removing It From Stock Indexes?

Strategy Made $19.5 Billion in Profit. So Why Is MSCI Removing It From Stock Indexes?

Strategy made $19.53 billion in profit last quarter. Yet MSCI, one of the world’s biggest providers of stock indexes, has decided Michael Saylor’s Bitcoin company no longer belongs in some of its major investment benchmarks.

MSCI’s November review lists “STRATEGY A”—the company’s MSTR shares—for deletion from the MSCI USA Index after trading closes November 30. That also removes the stock from broader indexes that include U.S. companies, such as the MSCI World and MSCI All Country World indexes.

That sounds technical, but the distinction matters: MSCI is not removing Strategy from the Nasdaq stock exchange, shutting down its business, or making it sell Bitcoin. It is taking MSTR out of stock lists that investment funds use to decide which companies to own.

Consider an ETF designed to copy the MSCI USA Index. When MSTR disappears from the list, the fund generally has to sell its shares, regardless of whether the fund manager likes Saylor’s strategy.

This is why it’s bad news for Strategy. It means less indirect exposition to investments.

MSCI adopted new rules in October for so-called non-operating companies. The idea is to keep investment vehicles—businesses that mainly hold financial assets—out of indexes meant to track operating companies. Its screening process considers a company’s operating assets and other financial measures.

MSCI’s deletion list does not spell out exactly which tests Strategy failed. The company, however, argues that raising capital, managing its Bitcoin treasury and issuing financial products amount to a genuine operating business.

In an August letter to MSCI, Strategy called the proposal “discriminatory, arbitrary, and misguided.” It argued that MSCI should be a “mirror of the market, not an arbiter of it.”

Strategy also maintains a software business, but Bitcoin now dominates its finances. The disagreement is whether its Bitcoin activity counts as running a company or mainly managing an investment portfolio.

Strategy’s latest quarterly earnings show $19.53 billion in net income. But that does not mean its software customers paid the company anything close to that amount.

Nearly all of its $20.91 billion in reported operating income came from a rise in the accounting value of its Bitcoin. Under rules adopted in 2025, changes in Bitcoin’s market price appear in Strategy’s earnings even when it has not sold the coins. A decline in Bitcoin can produce the opposite result.

Its software division, meanwhile, recorded $125.4 million in quarterly revenue, down 3% from a year earlier. Its $477.2 million in revenue for all of 2025 was slightly below the $486.3 million reported in 2019, before Strategy began buying Bitcoin.

The immediate risk is selling pressure on MSTR, not on Bitcoin itself. Strategy estimated that funds linked to MSCI indexes hold roughly 13 million of its shares, or 3.1% of its outstanding common stock. Not all of that necessarily translates into sudden sales, and Strategy says the amount is manageable.

But Strategy has repeatedly raised money by selling shares and other securities, then used those proceeds to buy Bitcoin. If its stock falls, selling the same number of new shares brings in less cash.

So the company would have to issue more shares to raise the same amount—or buy fewer Bitcoin.

That is why a stock-index decision could eventually matter to the crypto market. The exclusion does not force a Bitcoin sale, and it does not guarantee fewer purchases. It could, however, weaken a key source of funding for one of Bitcoin’s biggest corporate buyers.

#5016. FutureBit’s Apollo III Bitcoin Miner Hits Micro Center Shelves in Its First Brick-and-Mortar Launch

FutureBit is putting its Apollo III Full Node on sale Friday at four Micro Center stores, the first time customers can walk into a shop and take home one of the Brooklyn company’s bitcoin miners.

The compact home miner, which also runs a full bitcoin node, will be sold in Brooklyn, Miami, Tustin, California, and Austin, Texas, as those stores open Friday, FutureBit said in a release. The four-store launch coincides with the grand opening of Micro Center’s new Austin store, the chain’s 31st U.S. location and its third in Texas.

Customers will also be able to reserve a unit online for in-store pickup, the company said. It did not say how many units each store has in stock, or what Micro Center is charging for them.

Until now, buyers in North America had to order the machine from FutureBit’s website, where the company says units are in stock and ship in two to three days. Putting it on a computer-store shelf lets a customer look at the hardware, ask how it works and carry it out the same day.

“When we started FutureBit, we made weekly trips to the DIY electronics section at the Brooklyn Micro Center to buy parts,” said John Stefanopoulos, founder of FutureBit. “On Friday, someone can walk into that same store, ask how Bitcoin mining works and take home a miner we designed just down the street. We couldn’t be more excited to work with Micro Center on our first physical store launch.”

FutureBit’s own shop lists the Apollo III Full Node at $1,099.99 without a storage drive, $1,299.99 with 1 terabyte of SSD storage and $1,399.99 with 2 terabytes. A cheaper, miner-only “Standard” model starts at $899.99 but does not include the full node.

The Full Node is rated at up to 18 terahashes per second in Turbo mode, at about 325 watts. In Eco mode, it is listed at about 12 TH/s and 150 watts, with noise under 35 decibels. A Super Eco mode is listed at about 8 TH/s and 80 watts. Power can be adjusted from 50 to 400 watts, and Turbo mode is much louder, at about 55 decibels. Those power figures are measured at the board and can vary by 10%, the product page says.

The unit is a 6.5-by-6.5-by-6-inch cube that weighs 6.5 pounds, comes with a one-year limited warranty and is assembled in the United States. It uses new 3-nanometer, American-designed chips, a custom controller and 8 GB of memory, and it includes a built-in solo mining pool. Buyers can also point the miner at a standard bitcoin mining pool. FutureBit says the full node and solo-mining features require an SSD, which is not included in the $1,099.99 configuration.

Bitcoin Magazine covered the Apollo III’s debut in February, when FutureBit introduced the hardware as a way for individuals to run both a miner and a node at home. The point, the company has long argued, is not to compete with industrial mines on cost.

A single Apollo III at 18 TH/s is a sliver of the bitcoin network. A home-scale setup in that range still faces expected times to a solo block measured in centuries at recent difficulty, Bitcoin Magazine previously noted. Even so, a miner running through FutureBit’s Apollo Solo setup found block 973,262 on Oct. 26 and collected the full 3.154 bitcoin reward.

FutureBit, based in Brooklyn, has built consumer mining hardware since 2015. Stefanopoulos has framed store shelves as a way to put more hash rate and more nodes in living rooms. The company did not say whether the Micro Center test will expand beyond the four stores that began selling the Apollo III on Friday.

#5011. Thailand seeks $148,000 daily cap on certain stablecoin transfers to curb money laundering

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

The draft rules would limit individual customers’ withdrawals and deposits at a single regulated digital asset venue to 5 million baht (approximately $147,750) per day.

Thailand’s Securities and Exchange Commission is seeking public comments on a draft notification that would limit stablecoin transfers to crack down on money laundering.

The proposal, announced Thursday, would limit individual customers' withdrawals and deposits on regulated digital asset venues to 5 million baht (approximately $147,750) per operator, in either direction, per day. The draft regulation follows a public hearing in September on supervising stablecoin activity through licensed operators.

Beyond the amount limit, the draft rules require that stablecoins be transferred only between accounts or wallets belonging to the same person and prohibit transfers involving another person's wallets. However, the rules do not cover pure peer-to-peer, onchain transactions outside of registered platforms.

The agency would also require operators to comply with the Travel Rule by conducting customer profiling and screening, and use blockchain analytics tools to identify links to high-risk or watchlisted wallets.

“The value of stablecoins transferred into and out of a customer’s account must be commensurate with the customer’s source of income and financial position," the SEC stated.

Meanwhile, certain transfers would be exempt from the 5 million baht limit, such as movements between a customer’s own accounts on platforms under the SEC’s supervision, transfers by operators themselves for business purposes, stablecoin market-maker activity, and specific transactions related to digital token offerings and refunds. Certain activities approved by the Bank of Thailand will also be exempt from the limit.

These draft rules aim to prevent digital assets from being used for money laundering, cybercrime, or circumventing rules on international money transfers, the SEC stated.

The draft also introduces additional measures. Crypto exchanges would be required to disclose the names of their market makers and the assets for which they provide liquidity, along with enhanced screening of those firms.

Furthermore, brokers would be barred from using liquidity providers for stablecoin-baht trading pairs. Off-platform transactions by brokers and dealers would be subject to a minimum threshold of 3 million baht ($88,528), and operators would have to disclose the trading prices for such deals.

The SEC is currently seeking public comments on the draft notification, with Nov. 26 as the deadline.

The requirement builds on steps Thai authorities had already taken. The country’s central bank and securities regulator had reportedly started using data analytics to scrutinize unusual USDT trading, as part of a wider push to close gaps that enable money laundering and other “grey economy” activity.

#5009. North Korea Stole $400 Million in Crypto Using Deepfake Video Calls, DOJ Says

North Korea Stole $400 Million in Crypto Using Deepfake Video Calls, DOJ Says

North Korean hackers have stolen more than $400 million in cryptocurrency over the past 18 months using a social-engineering scheme built on secretly recorded footage and AI deepfakes, the U.S. Justice Department said Thursday, as it announced the seizure of the infrastructure behind the operation.

The scheme, which the FBI calls “FaceStealer,” turns video conference calls into a trap. According to the DOJ, hackers lure targets into meetings using accounts stolen from previous victims, then play prerecorded webcam footage of trusted contacts to simulate their presence and win the target’s confidence.

The group also generates deepfake videos of well-known figures in the crypto and related industries, using AI to make the ruse more convincing.

Once a target is at ease, the attackers manufacture a fake technical glitch, such as claiming the person can’t be heard, and offer a link to “fix” it, which instead installs malware.

From there, the hackers can drain crypto wallets or exploit the victim’s access to other systems, sometimes waiting months or more than a year before striking. The FBI said it seized over 900 webcam recordings of FaceStealer victims under a federal warrant.

The DOJ tied the operation to North Korean groups known variously as Sapphire Sleet, BlueNoroff and APT38, among others, and warned the hackers have increasingly targeted open-source software developers in an apparent bid to enable supply-chain attacks.

The announcement came paired with an update on the record-breaking Binance hack. The department said it has now obtained court authorization to seize or restrain more than $1.2 billion of the roughly $6.4 billion stolen from the exchange on Oct. 29, part of over $2.7 billion frozen so far.

The FBI attributed that theft to the North Korean group TraderTraitor, and the regime has been laundering the proceeds at speed, spinning up a new wallet roughly every 25 seconds. North Korea has denied involvement, calling the FBI’s finding a political provocation.

The actions underscore how central crypto theft has become to Pyongyang’s finances. The U.S. recently sanctioned 11 people over a North Korean IT-worker scheme that moved millions in crypto, and researchers have cataloged the many ways the regime’s hackers break into crypto firms.

Officials said efforts to trace and recover the stolen Binance funds are ongoing.

#5006. UK, Singapore, and Thailand central banks complete foreign exchange settlement trial linking traditional and tokenized systems

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

The Reserve Bank of Australia and Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas participated as observers, while the Bank of England plans to launch a live synchronisation interface in 2028.

Three central banks have completed tests of a cross-border foreign exchange settlement system connecting traditional payment infrastructure with distributed ledger technology.

In a joint statement on Friday, the Bank of England, Monetary Authority of Singapore, and Bank of Thailand said they conducted the experiments using a prototype developed by Partior, which coordinated payment-versus-payment (PvP) settlement and multilateral net FX transactions across their test environments.

The three central banks are working under Project Meridian FX APAC, announced last November. The project encompassed multiple currencies, technologies, settlement infrastructures, and time zones, with the Reserve Bank of Australia and Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas also participating as observers, the banks said.

According to the statement, Partio's system matched settlement instructions, coordinated the reservation of funds, monitored payment readiness, and initiated settlement.

The experiment also examined multilateral netting, which allows banks to offset payments against one another to reduce the liquidity needed for settlement.

However, the accompanying policy report identified questions around operational resilience, settlement finality, governance, liability, and cross-border data sharing. It also warned that additional functions, including holding funds or calculating net positions, could change an operator's regulatory responsibilities.

Tom Mutton, the BOE's executive director of payments, innovation and fintech, said the project provided "practical evidence of how synchronized settlement could help reduce risk and improve efficiency in cross-border FX transactions."

The BOE plans to launch a live synchronization interface in 2028. Findings from Project Meridian FX APAC will inform further work on synchronized settlement.

It’s one of those dresses that looks just as good styled casually as it does dressed up a bit.

It’s also incredibly versatile. The lightweight cotton makes it comfortable enough for daytime exploring while the longer sleeves give a little extra coverage when the temperature dips. It’s easy to throw on with sandals during the day or dress up with boots or jewelry at night—and just as easy to pack, thanks to that forgiving, wrinkle-resistant texture.

Meet the perfect mini dress. I own it in black, and it always looks incredibly chic—whether I’m dressing it up with heels for a city dinner or keeping it casual with sandals for daytime plans. It’s one of my favorite pieces because it feels polished no matter how you style it—coming in clutch for travel.

The fabric plays a big role in that versatility. It's made from a polyester crepe that has a subtle texture and is naturally wrinkle-resistant—ideal for tossing in a suitcase without a second thought. It holds its shape well and doesn't cling, giving it a clean, streamlined look straight out of your bag.

It has a classic, body-skimming silhouette that gently follows your shape without feeling tight or restrictive. The mini length hits at about mid-thigh, while the boat neckline adds a classy feel that instantly upgrades the overall look. It’s simple, but in that very polished, well-designed way.

It checks all the boxes for travel. The Bond Dress packs down easily, comes out looking polished, and can be styled in multiple ways depending on your itinerary. If there's a downside, it's that the streamlined fit doesn't leave much room for built-in functionality like shorts or roomy pockets, but the trade-off is a sleek, goes-with-anything mini you’ll reach for again and again.

The Dylan Mini Dress earns its spot as the most stylish pick thanks to its ultra-flattering shape and the prettiest range of colors and patterns. It has that slightly romantic feel that instantly dresses up your outfit, whether you’re heading to dinner or just wandering a new city. I always get compliments when I wear this dress (it was a major hit during my trip to Mallorca)—and it looks just as good in photos as it does in person.

The fit is where it really stands out. It has a flattering scoop neckline trimmed with delicate lace, plus a fitted bodice that dips slightly at the waist to help elongate your torso. From there, it flows into a long, airy skirt that moves beautifully as you walk. Adjustable straps let you customize the fit, and the built-in bra with removable pads adds support without the need for extra layers—always a win when packing light.

In terms of length, it hits a few inches above the ankles for that easy, breezy feel, and it comes in petite, regular, and tall options so you can find your ideal fit. The longer length gives it a slightly dressier edge, while still feeling relaxed enough for daytime wear. Despite the longer length, I don’t have any issues packing this dress in my suitcase when I pop it into a packing cube.

Style-wise, it leans pretty and girly in the best way. It’s perfect for summer travel or warm-weather destinations, but also transitions nicely into cooler conditions with a simple cardigan layered on top. The only con? Popular colors and patterns tend to sell out fast—so if you see a style available in your size, I recommend snagging it ASAP.

Since traveling involves lots of packing, travel expert Addie Bell says to look for wrinkle-resistant materials like spandex, nylon, or polyester. These fabrics are great for maintaining a polished look after being packed in a suitcase. Travel days often include a lot of walking, so you'll also want to make sure your dress's fabric is breathable—cotton and linen are great choices, but they are prone to wrinkling.

If you’re only traveling with a carry-on or trying to maximize storage, stick to neutral tones like black, navy, white, and beige, which are versatile and easy to mix and match with other wardrobe pieces. "Subtle patterns can also help hide wrinkles and stains, making the dress more travel-friendly," says Bell. But bright colors can add a fun, vibrant touch. "I always recommend sticking within a similar color palette to ensure they match other items you’re bringing.”

#5002. From $6 to $6.9 million: Two dormant Bitcoin addresses wake up to move 100 BTC after more than 16 years

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

The two sends took place just over two minutes apart, and a later transaction combined coins from both transfers into a single address.

Two Bitcoin addresses that had sat dormant for more than 16 years moved 100 BTC on Friday morning, worth approximately $6.89 million, according to onchain data.

The first address sent nearly 50 BTC to one address and 0.01 BTC to another at 4:08 a.m. UTC. Just over two minutes later, the second address sent nearly 49 BTC to one address and 1 BTC to another. Both sets of coins came from block rewards mined in September 2010, data from blockchain explorer Mempool shows. Onchain monitoring platform Whale Alert first reported the moves, estimating that each 50 BTC reward was worth about $3 when received in 2010.

By 4:48 a.m. UTC, about 20 BTC from the first transfer and 39 BTC from the second had been consolidated at a new address starting "bc1qj5." Some 30 BTC sits at another new address starting "bc1qqs," 10 BTC at "bc1qds," and 1 BTC at "bc1qce" at the time of writing.

The reason for the transfers, the identity of the wallets' owners, and whether the two original outputs had the same owner remain unknown.

With bitcoin Bitcoin (BTC) currently trading for around $69,000, according to The Block's prices page, the value of the bitcoin the addresses transferred has risen more than 1.15 million times since 2010.

Mempool labels both 50 BTC inputs as pay-to-public-key, or P2PK. The four addresses that received the coins on Friday all start with bc1q, a prefix used by newer native SegWit (P2WPKH) addresses. Older Bitcoin addresses include pay-to-public-key-hash (P2PKH) addresses starting with 1 and pay-to-script-hash (P2SH) addresses starting with 3. The latest Taproot (P2TR) address format starts with bc1p.

Other early bitcoin holdings have moved to newer address formats after years of dormancy, and several addresses named in a New York lawsuit over allegedly abandoned bitcoin have moved funds recently after the plaintiffs sent onchain notices.

Five 50 BTC block rewards mined in April 2010 went untouched for about 15 years before they moved to two SegWit addresses in July 2025. The coins were worth about $29.6 million at the time. A March 2024 transaction combined 40 mining rewards from 2010, totaling 2,000 BTC worth nearly $140 million.

#5000. Republican Senator Wants to Freeze AI Data Center Boom as Congress Pushes to Expand It

Republican Senator Wants to Freeze AI Data Center Boom as Congress Pushes to Expand It

Republican Senator Josh Hawley wants Congress to hit the brakes on new data centers, just as lawmakers are moving forward with legislation intended to make building the infrastructure behind America's AI boom easier.

The Missouri senator called for a nationwide moratorium Wednesday, listing it among five priorities for Senate Republicans during the six weeks before Democrats take control of the chamber.

“Senate Republicans trying to figure out what to do in the next 6 weeks?” Hawley wrote on X. His answer included a moratorium on data centers, alongside defunding Planned Parenthood, suspending the gas tax and other Republican priorities.

A spokesperson told Politico that Hawley wants a federal pause until Congress passes a “bill of rights giving taxpayers guarantees of no rate increases.” Hawley has not presented detailed legislation specifying which projects would stop or how long the freeze would last.

Data centers are the warehouses packed with powerful computers that train and operate services such as ChatGPT. Building more AI systems means installing more servers, which requires additional electricity, cooling equipment and often upgrades to local power grids.

Senate Republicans trying to figure out what to do in the next 6 weeks? Here you go:DEFUND Planned ParenthoodMORATORIUM on data centersSUSPEND the gas tax FUND rural hospitals SAVE AMERICA ACT

— Josh Hawley (@HawleyMO) November 11, 2026

The scale helps explain the concern. U.S. data centers consumed an estimated 183 terawatt-hours of electricity in 2024, according to figures cited by Pew, and that could climb to 426 by 2030. In other words, their annual electricity demand could more than double in six years.

On Monday, the Senate voted 73-25 to advance debate on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, a proposal backed by lawmakers from both parties and President Donald Trump's administration.

The bill would speed federal reviews for energy projects and transmission lines, helping bring new power supplies online. It would also require data center operators to pay the additional grid costs their projects create, rather than shifting those expenses onto ordinary electricity customers.

In practical terms, Congress is considering how to keep construction moving without making households subsidize it. Hawley is asking lawmakers to stop new construction until consumer protections are in place.

His position is not entirely new. In February, Hawley introduced the GRID Act with Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal, seeking to make new data centers obtain electricity from their own sources rather than relying on existing grid supplies.

He now joins independent Senator Bernie Sanders and Democratic Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez in publicly supporting a national pause. Their moratorium proposal goes further, calling for rules addressing AI's effects on workers and public safety as well as the environment.

The politics have shifted quickly. In the November 3 elections, voters backed restrictions on data center development across the country, including local bans and measures requiring public approval before construction.

A Pew Research Center analysis published Wednesday found 60% of Americans uncomfortable with a new data center in their area, including 54% of Republicans and 68% of Democrats. Another survey found 58% disliked political leaders who support building data centers near them.

Opponents worry about rising bills, water consumption and noise. Cities have already imposed restrictions, while OpenAI recently promised to cover electricity and grid costs at future campuses it owns and operates.

Industry supporters see a bigger economic risk. BlackRock CEO Larry Fink warned last month that a construction moratorium could trigger a recession because so much investment now depends on AI infrastructure.

A federal construction freeze could delay the additional computing capacity that AI companies expect to bring online, along with the power infrastructure built to support it. Existing data centers would not necessarily shut down, but the scope of Hawley's proposed moratorium remains undefined.

Hawley's call does not freeze a single project, and he has not said whether he would support the Sanders bill. For now, the Senate is debating legislation to speed infrastructure approvals, not legislation to ban new data centers.

#4997. Ethereum and Layer 1s Explained

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

Smart Contracts, Gas, and Blockchain Trade-offs

Ethereum is a Layer 1 blockchain designed for programmable applications. It uses accounts, smart contracts, the Ethereum Virtual Machine, ETH, gas fees, and Proof of Stake to support decentralized applications and compete within a wider ecosystem of Layer 1 blockchains.

While Bitcoin is viewed as digital gold, an inflation hedge, or digital money, other crypto entrepreneurs wanted to push the envelope further. A few years after Bitcoin, Ethereum outlined infrastructure for smart contracts, decentralized applications, and new financial systems. This guide explains Ethereum’s premise, ecosystem, advantages, and the hurdles Layer 1 blockchains face.

The lesson summaries below give a short overview of the full course content. Take the full interactive Ethereum & Layer 1s 101 course to explore each lesson in more depth through guided explanations, examples, and activities.

Positions Ethereum as the next step after Bitcoin, adding smart contracts, decentralized applications, and new approaches to Layer 1 design.

Explains how Ethereum made blockchains programmable through smart contracts and decentralized applications.

Covers externally owned accounts, contract accounts, account balances, Bitcoin’s UTXO contrast, and the Ethereum Virtual Machine.

Shows how Ethereum supports automated financial services such as trading, lending, borrowing, and collateral management.

Introduces ETH, gas, gwei, network congestion, base and priority fees, and the role of EIP-1559.

Explains Ethereum’s move away from Proof of Work and the roles of validators, staking, and slashing.

Lesson 6 - Ethereum Improvement Proposals

Describes how EIPs move from a documented idea through public review and possible network implementation.

Compares Ethereum with other Layer 1 and Layer 0 designs through the blockchain trilemma.

Connects native tokens and blockspace to validator incentives, wallets, RPC nodes, oracles, and other Web3 infrastructure.

Introduces the scalability problem and explains why Layer 2 systems are the natural next topic.

Bitcoin proved that a decentralized network could maintain money and a transaction ledger without a central authority. Ethereum extended that idea by making the blockchain programmable. Instead of only transferring value, Ethereum made it possible to run code on-chain.

The core innovation is the smart contract: a piece of code that runs on a blockchain and automatically executes predefined actions when specific conditions are met. In the vending-machine analogy, you insert money, and the machine dispenses your snack without needing human intervention.

Smart contracts make decentralized applications, or dApps, possible. These applications function without traditional intermediaries, with use cases that range from financial services to games.

To understand how a vending machine can live inside a blockchain, start with Ethereum’s accounts. Ethereum has two main account types. Externally owned accounts, or EOAs, are user-controlled accounts secured by a private key. They can send and receive ETH, interact with smart contracts, and initiate transactions.

Contract accounts are controlled by smart-contract code, not private keys. They cannot initiate transactions on their own. Instead, they act in response to transactions sent by EOAs or other contracts, executing predefined code when triggered.

Ethereum also uses an account-based model, where balances are stored directly in accounts, similar to a bank ledger. This differs from Bitcoin’s UTXO model, which tracks individual transaction outputs. The account-based approach makes it easier for smart contracts to check balances and interact with users or other contracts.

Smart contracts execute inside a virtual environment called the Ethereum Virtual Machine, or EVM. The EVM resembles a universal translation service: just as a translation service helps everyone in a multilingual meeting understand the same message, the EVM provides a framework where smart contracts run the same way on every node in the network.

That consistency matters because every participating node needs to agree on what the smart contract did. Ethereum’s application-focused account model and the EVM together power decentralized applications, including the broader ecosystem of decentralized finance.

Ethereum’s infrastructure was not set up this way by accident. The aim was to go beyond decentralized money and expand how financial services could work. This is where decentralized finance, or DeFi, comes in.

DeFi aims to replace or rework financial functions such as lending, borrowing, trading, and earning interest with blockchain-based protocols. Instead of relying on a bank or broker, users interact with smart contracts that enforce rules automatically.

ETH, or Ether, is the fuel or incentive that powers the Ethereum network. Every interaction, from sending tokens to deploying smart contracts, requires ETH to pay gas fees.

Gas fees are the cost that comes with every transaction or interaction with a smart contract. They serve two main purposes: they compensate validators for keeping the network running, and they help prevent spam by making every action on the network carry a cost.

Gas fees work like a toll system. Ethereum has limited blockspace, and when more users want to use the network at the same time, the cost of getting into the next block can rise.

Gas prices are commonly quoted in gwei. Under EIP-1559, a transaction fee includes a network-determined base fee and may include a priority fee for the validator. This gives users a clearer fee structure, although the total cost still changes with demand and the amount of computation required.

Ethereum initially operated with Proof of Work, where miners validate transactions by solving complex computational puzzles. It later transitioned to Proof of Stake in the upgrade known as The Merge.

Proof of Stake works differently. Instead of miners competing with hardware, validators are selected to create new blocks, with their role tied to ETH staked as collateral. Staking acts as a financial commitment to follow the rules, because dishonest behavior can put a validator’s staked funds at risk through slashing.

Ethereum Improvement Proposals, or EIPs, are formal proposal documents that describe potential changes to the Ethereum network. They resemble blueprints for upgrading a city bridge: an idea is written down, reviewed, debated, and, if accepted, implemented as a network upgrade.

Ethereum was one of the first major highways built for smart contracts, but as more people used it, traffic jams and higher tolls became common. That opened the door for other blockchain platforms to emerge with different design choices.

Chains such as Bitcoin and Ethereum are called Layer 1 chains because they are base, independent networks that do not rely on another blockchain for operation. Other Layer 1s may optimize for speed, cost, decentralization, developer experience, or specific use cases.

The common challenge is the blockchain trilemma: improving two of the major cornerstones often comes at the cost of the third.

Layer 1 tokens such as ETH are not only traded assets. They play operational roles in paying for blockspace, incentivizing validators, and securing the network through rewards and fees.

Other important topics include Web3 infrastructure: wallets as user access points, middleware such as RPC nodes and oracles, and security/audit services that help applications interact with blockchain networks. These surrounding tools fill needed roles around the base blockchain.

Balancing the blockchain trilemma is difficult. To support broader adoption, scalability becomes a critical problem: without effective scaling solutions, blockchains can become too slow or too expensive for everyday use.

In a city-road analogy, a single-lane road works when only a few people drive, but if everyone starts driving at once, the road becomes gridlocked. Blockchains face a similar challenge when demand rises faster than the base layer can process activity.

Ethereum expanded blockchain use cases by introducing smart contracts and decentralized applications.

Ethereum uses EOAs, contract accounts, an account-based model, and the EVM to make smart-contract execution consistent across the network.

ETH is the native currency used to pay gas fees, which price computation and help prevent spam.

Proof of Stake replaces miners with validators who stake ETH and can be penalized for dishonest behavior.

EIPs provide a structured way to propose and coordinate Ethereum upgrades.

Alternative Layer 1s make different trade-offs across decentralization, scalability, and security.

Scaling is the natural next topic because base-layer blockchains face throughput and cost limits as adoption grows.

This 101 subject is designed for readers who already have a basic grasp of Bitcoin and blockchain terminology. It helps to understand what a blockchain is, why decentralization matters, how wallets and private keys work, and why blockchains need consensus before moving into Ethereum and Layer 1 design.

Ethereum: A Layer 1 blockchain designed to support smart contracts and decentralized applications.

Layer 1: A base blockchain network that does not rely on another chain for its core operation.

Smart contract: Code that runs on a blockchain and automatically executes predefined actions when conditions are met.

dApp: A decentralized application that uses smart contracts instead of relying only on traditional intermediaries.

EOA: An externally owned account controlled by a private key.

Contract account: An Ethereum account controlled by smart-contract code.

EVM: The Ethereum Virtual Machine, where smart-contract logic executes consistently across the network.

Gas fee: The cost paid in ETH to process a transaction or smart-contract interaction.

Gwei: A small unit of ETH used to price gas.

Proof of Stake: A consensus model where validators stake ETH and participate in block creation and validation.

Slashing: A penalty mechanism that can reduce a validator’s stake for dishonest or faulty behavior.

EIP: An Ethereum Improvement Proposal describing a possible network change.

Blockchain trilemma: The trade-off among decentralization, scalability, and security.

Web3 infrastructure: Wallets, RPC nodes, oracles, and related services that help users and applications interact with blockchains.

After Ethereum & Layer 1s, useful next topics include Scaling & Layer 2s, DeFi, Market Structure and the deeper Ethereum & Layer 1s 201 guide.

Bitcoin primarily introduced decentralized digital money and a transaction ledger, while Ethereum made blockchains programmable through smart contracts and decentralized applications.

Gas fees are the cost of processing transactions or smart-contract interactions. They compensate validators and help prevent spam by pricing computation.

#4996. 8 Best Travel Pants for Women, Tested by Travel Experts and Editors
